brief.head: Credentials not needed
brief.text: When Amit Varma says hire the best, Ajay Shah said, he does not mean IIT or IIM badges but knowl­edge, char­ac­ter and con­nec­tion with the world. {103-C12}

brief.head: Dream big, hire well
brief.text: Firms that po­si­tion them­selves as nar­row bean coun­ters get av­er­age em­ploy­ees, Ajay Shah said. Those chas­ing big au­da­cious dreams are more likely to at­tract re­mark­able peo­ple. {103-C06}

brief.head: Who sets strategy?
brief.text: In India, Ajay Shah said, strat­egy tends to rest with a fam­ily pro­moter or a CEO. The in­sti­tu­tion of the board is only barely un­der­stood. {#boards}

brief.head: From cause to racket
brief.text: Ajay Shah of­fered a one-liner with “ab­so­lutely noth­ing to do with this episode”: every great idea starts out as a cause, then be­comes a move­ment, then a racket. {103-J04}

brief.head: The glory of big firms
brief.text: The top 20,000 non-financial firms are pretty much the Indian econ­omy, Ajay Shah said. “All the glory of mod­ern cap­i­tal­ism is ac­tu­ally in the large com­pa­nies.” {103-C09}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma’s thirteen rules for starting a business
lead.head: Mind your own business

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 103

body: The last episode ended with a bias for ac­tion. This one picked up there, with Amit Varma lay­ing out thir­teen more pieces of ad­vice for any­one who might start a busi­ness, and Ajay Shah adding his own.
Even if you ex­pect to be a banker all your life, Shah said, there is merit in kick­ing your­self and think­ing: let’s start a busi­ness. Building one, he ar­gued, makes you a bet­ter em­ployee too.
Much of Varma’s ad­vice came from clips of founders and in­vestors such as Jeff Bezos, Sam Altman, Jensen Huang and Naval Ravikant.
## From project to com­pany
Start as a spe­cial­ist, Varma said, but be­come a gen­er­al­ist once the project be­comes a com­pany. {103-C01}

Then think from first prin­ci­ples. Elon Musk, he said, priced a bat­tery from its raw ma­te­ri­als and cut its cost from $600 to $80 per kilo­watt hour, while ex­perts said bat­ter­ies could not be any cheaper.
“All progress hap­pens be­cause some­one chal­lenged the con­ven­tional think­ing and on some mar­gin the con­ven­tional think­ing was wrong,” Varma said. {103-C03}

Then the cus­tomer, who is never to be blamed for a product’s fail­ings. Then the prod­uct it­self. Varma, who says he does 100 per cent prod­uct and 0 per cent mar­ket­ing, quoted Kevin Hale: “Marketing is a tax you pay for not mak­ing your prod­uct awe­some.”
Then a mis­sion big­ger than your­self, and a long hori­zon. “A long term com­mit­ment is the only ar­bi­trage op­por­tu­nity left in the mar­ket,” he said, quot­ing Altman.
## The peo­ple and the work
Choose co-founders above all for in­tegrity, Varma said, and em­ploy­ees for val­ues first, ap­ti­tude sec­ond and skill third.

Hard work, he said, is non-negotiable. Mandated 70-hour weeks are wrong, but vol­un­tar­ily he could give every hour of his week when he is not sleep­ing. Burnout, he thinks, comes from wor­ry­ing, pro­cras­ti­nat­ing and over­think­ing, not from work.
And firms must build a cul­ture of truth-telling, be­cause hu­mans did not evolve for it. “We’ve evolved to get along with each other,” Varma said. “We’ve not evolved to tell the truth.” {103-C14}
Shah tied this to what he called the cen­tral cri­sis of firms: in large, im­pe­rial com­pa­nies, knowl­edge about cus­tomers and pro­duc­tion does not bub­ble up to the top.
## Simple, proud and true

The last rules were about val­ues. Simplicity first: Robinhood’s one screen, one but­ton, one ac­tion, and Stripe’s five-minute in­te­gra­tion. “The evo­lu­tion to great­ness is al­ways an evo­lu­tion to­wards sim­plic­ity,” Varma said. {103-C16}

Then pro­fes­sional pride, in work that no­body else will see. And fi­nally Warren Buffett’s inner score­card: his father’s les­son that you judge your­self by your own val­ues, not by money, suc­cess or what peo­ple write about you.
“If you don’t score high on your inner score­card, noth­ing is worth it,” Varma said. {103-C18}
Shah’s rec­om­men­da­tion flowed from that: Clayton Christensen’s *How Will You Measure Your Life?*, “a beau­ti­ful, sim­ple book”.

Varma, a lit­er­a­ture stu­dent, said his twenty-year-old self would have been sur­prised by his con­clu­sion: that some of our finest thinkers, among them Paul Graham and Naval Ravikant, are from the world of busi­ness.
He closed by urg­ing view­ers to share the episodes, like and sub­scribe, then caught him­self. “Did I just say I will never do mar­ket­ing? I will never do mar­ket­ing, don’t bother.”

second.label: Never blame the user
second.head: University challenge
second.deck: Larry Page’s demo to Excite, and the lesson Aravind Srinivas drew from it

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Larry Page’s demo to Excite

body: In the late 1990s, Amit Varma re­called, the search en­gines in­cluded Yahoo, Excite and Ask Jeeves. {103-J07} Larry Page took his PageRank tech­nol­ogy to Excite to sell it. His en­gine, asked for “uni­ver­sity”, found Harvard and Stanford; Excite found ran­dom junk.

Nobody types “uni­ver­sity”, the Excite ex­ec­u­tive ob­jected; a proper user would ask for the best Ivy League uni­ver­sity in America. Page’s an­swer, in Varma’s telling: “You’re gaslight­ing the user. You’re say­ing the user is stupid.” {103-S02}

Aravind Srinivas of Perplexity, who tells the story, learnt from it. When his mother com­plained about her re­sults, he nearly told her to fix the gram­mar of her ques­tion, then stopped him­self: the fault was his, not hers.

quote.text: The prob­lem is not with the user, the prob­lem is with you.

third.head: Gates tunes out the radio

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Bill Gates’s missing car radio

body: Mike Moritz was being driven to the air­port by Bill Gates, prob­a­bly in the early 1980s, Amit Varma guessed. Where the car radio should have been, there was an empty slot. {103-R25}
Had some­one stolen it? “No, no, no, no one stole it, I took it out,” Gates said. “Because if I lis­ten to the radio, that’ll take away my time for think­ing about Microsoft.” {103-S04}

Varma paired it with Jensen Huang, who does not wear a watch be­cause “now is the most im­por­tant time”. Obsession, in Apoorva Mehta’s def­i­ni­tion, means the com­pany is the last thing on your mind at night and the first in the morn­ing.
Hard work is non-negotiable, Varma ar­gued. A man­dated 70-hour week is wrong; a cho­sen one is fine. “The path to ex­cel­lence al­ways comes with hard work.” {103-C13}

p2.title: The founder’s rulebook
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s advice for anyone starting a business, argued over chapter by chapter with Ajay Shah

quote.text: So when you’re an em­ployee, you’re being told to shut up, be nar­row, ex­e­cute, ex­e­cute, ex­e­cute. But at the lead­er­ship level, it’s up­side down.

box.title: Where the advice came from
box.text: Jeff Bezos turns up more than any­one in Amit Varma’s ad­vice, which came mostly from short clips of founders and in­vestors. Many were found on Startup Archive, an Instagram ac­count Varma fol­lows. {103-R41}

sections.label: The first rule
sections.head: What do they know of X?
sections.caption: being a generalist
body: Start as a spe­cial­ist, and be­come a gen­er­al­ist the day your project turns into a com­pany. That was Amit Varma’s first piece of ad­vice, taken from a video by Sam Altman. {103-R02}

Larry Page and Sergey Brin were spe­cial­ists while PageRank was a project, he said. A founder must step back and look at the world. Varma reached for Rudyard Kipling and C.L.R. James: what do they know of cricket who only cricket knows? {103-C01}
Ajay Shah noted that Google’s early slo­gan was not to be the best search en­gine but to or­gan­ise the world’s in­for­ma­tion, an am­bi­tion that opened it to all kinds of ad­ja­cen­cies.

He warned that ven­ture cap­i­tal­ists often keep founders to their last pitch deck. Varma re­called Vinod Khosla’s claim that sev­enty per cent of ven­ture cap­i­tal­ists add neg­a­tive value. {#negative} The bur­den of learn­ing falls on the founder.
## Strategy is up­side down

Shah then turned to the em­ployee. The most im­por­tant think­ing in any firm, he said, is strat­egy: who are we, what are our ca­pa­bil­i­ties, what amaz­ing things can we do that the world will like? Marching or­ders flow from that down to the di­vi­sions.
An em­ployee is told to shut up, be nar­row and ex­e­cute, Shah said. At the lead­er­ship level, it is up­side down. {103-C02}
~ A leader must keep won­der­ing, re-evaluating and chang­ing his mind. That is why, he ar­gued, think­ing like a founder makes even a banker a bet­ter em­ployee.

quote.text: So when you’re an em­ployee, you’re being told to shut up, be nar­row, ex­e­cute, ex­e­cute, ex­e­cute. But at the lead­er­ship level, it’s up­side down.

sections.label: The third rule
sections.head: Small is a luxury
sections.caption: acting small
body: In the last episode, Amit Varma urged founders to be in­ward-driven. Once the busi­ness ex­ists, he said, the cus­tomer mat­ters most, and the dan­ger is notic­ing com­peti­tors more than cus­tomers.

Jeff Bezos, he said, de­cided very early on to focus on cus­tomers and not com­peti­tors. {#customers} He also pre­ferred to ask what would stay the same: ten or twenty years on, peo­ple will still want lower prices, bet­ter value and faster de­liv­ery.

Above all, never blame the user. Founders get car­ried away by the Kool-Aid of their own prod­uct, Varma said, and dis­miss the critic who doesn’t get it. He cast Ajay Shah as that critic, and Shah sup­plied the jab him­self: “He’s a Unix com­mand line user.” {103-J06}
## When small, act small
Garry Tan’s ad­vice, Varma said, is that small com­pa­nies should not mimic the pol­ish of big ones, with a front page like Microsoft’s. Act small, and get close to the cus­tomer.
In the startup he ran be­fore Y Combinator, Tan and his team an­swered cus­tomer emails per­son­ally. One day of the week, it was the CEO’s duty to an­swer every com­plaint him­self. {#tanemails}
~ When you have a hun­dred or two hun­dred cus­tomers, Varma said, you can speak to every one of them. When you grow big­ger, you can’t.

quote.text: small­ness is a lux­ury that al­lows you to get that in­ti­macy with your cus­tomer and build an in­cred­i­ble prod­uct.

sections.label: The fourth rule
sections.head: The tax on a dull product
sections.caption: product over marketing
body: Amit Varma’s fourth rule is close to his heart: don’t ob­sess over mar­ket­ing. He quoted Kevin Hale of Y Combinator: “Marketing is a tax you pay for not mak­ing your prod­uct awe­some.” {103-C05}

When peo­ple ask why he doesn’t cut clips of his shows for YouTube or Instagram, his an­swer has been that a good prod­uct is the best mar­ket­ing. He built *The Seen and the Unseen* that way, he said, and thinks he has been proved right.

He does 100 per cent prod­uct and 0 per cent mar­ket­ing. There may be an op­ti­mum, he con­ceded: with 5 or 10 per cent mar­ket­ing, more of his tribe might find him. {#optimum} But he will not spend his lim­ited band­width find­ing it.
## The dan­ger in the mind­set

Marketing is not bad, Varma said. The dan­ger is that a mar­ket­ing ori­en­ta­tion takes over your think­ing, pulling you to­wards the low­est com­mon de­nom­i­na­tor and short-term grat­i­fi­ca­tion in­stead of build­ing some­thing great for the long term.
The same goes for peo­ple. Naval Ravikant calls net­work­ing over­rated: do some­thing great and your net­work will emerge. {103-R08}

~ Varma found the same. The won­der­ful peo­ple he has come to know came through his pod­casts, not con­fer­ences or trade fairs. First make it awe­some, he tells would-be founders, and ev­ery­thing will work out.

quote.text: Your tribe will even­tu­ally find you.

sections.label: The sixth rule
sections.head: A plan worth tearing up
sections.caption: thinking long-term
body: “A long term com­mit­ment is the only ar­bi­trage op­por­tu­nity left in the mar­ket,” Amit Varma said, quot­ing Sam Altman. {103-C07} Most peo­ple think about the next quar­ter; the long view is your edge.

Jeff Bezos wrote a 30-page busi­ness plan for Amazon know­ing, as the VCs did, that it would fall apart on con­tact with re­al­ity. Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face, as Ajay Shah put it, sup­ply­ing Mike Tyson’s line. “But that ex­er­cise of writ­ing thirty pages is im­por­tant,” Varma said, “be­cause it clar­i­fies your think­ing.” {103-S08}

Vinod Khosla’s rule is to be ob­sti­nate about your vi­sion and flex­i­ble about your tac­tics. Eric Schmidt even rec­om­mends five-year plans. The hosts are no fans of those for India’s econ­omy, Varma said, be­cause an econ­omy can’t be cen­trally planned; a com­pany can. {103-J10}
## Rethink HR

Shah has met many se­nior man­agers who preach long-term think­ing while HR pays bonuses on nar­row tar­gets over a quar­ter or a year. Then why would any­one take more risks? If your peo­ple are short-sighted, he said, it is your fault. {103-C08}

~ His fix is to speak in com­pound­ing num­bers that ex­cite peo­ple: 5x in five years, 10x in ten. A 14 per cent nom­i­nal growth a year for five years is a dou­bling. {#doubling} That pushes man­agers to lay the foun­da­tions of a big­ger firm.

quote.text: The bane of India is short term think­ing.

sections.label: The seventh rule
sections.head: Teach your founders well
sections.caption: choosing a co-founder
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah for his favourite Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song, fish­ing for *Teach Your Children*. Shah of­fered *Helpless* and *Southern Cross*. “See, we don’t script any­thing,” Varma said, and moved on: choose your founders well. {103-J11}

Patrick Collison, he said, thinks start­ing with some­one you are close to is a fea­ture, not a bug. Brian Chesky’s rea­son: you will spend more time with your co-founder than with your spouse. {103-R19}
Ten or fif­teen years ago, with his male macho ego, Varma would have thought win­ning an ar­gu­ment was ev­ery­thing. Today what mat­ters to him is the re­la­tion­ship.

Naval Ravikant looks for high in­tel­li­gence, high en­ergy and high in­tegrity, and of those, by far the most im­por­tant is in­tegrity. {#integrity} Garry Tan warns against co-CEOs, be­cause every de­ci­sion below them slows down.
## Arguing to learn

Shah added that a great part­ner­ship brings dif­fer­ent knowl­edge to the table, and both part­ners do Bayesian up­dat­ing. It hardly mat­ters which de­ci­sion is taken, be­cause both come out stronger. The point, he said, is to jointly build a the­ory of the world and of the firm. {103-C11}
~ People too sure of them­selves to up­date, Shah said, have a se­ri­ous char­ac­ter de­fect.

quote.text: And the pur­pose of the dis­agree­ment ac­tu­ally is to build a model of the world.

sections.label: The tenth rule
sections.head: Clubbed for the truth
sections.caption: optimising for truth-telling
body: Jeff Bezos’s ad­vice, which Amit Varma made his own, is to op­ti­mise for truth-telling. Humans are so­cial an­i­mals, Varma said. A truth-teller could be clubbed to death in a tribe. {103-C14}

So or­gan­i­sa­tions drift, by de­fault, to­wards def­er­ence up the hi­er­ar­chy and po­lite­ness among peers. Firms must build mech­a­nisms and a cul­ture against this. One is Bezos’s prac­tice of dis­agree and com­mit, from his in­ter­view with Lex Fridman: argue, then fully own the de­ci­sion, with no “I told you so” later. {103-R34}
## The im­pe­rial firm

Ajay Shah called in­for­ma­tion the cen­tral cri­sis of firms. Knowledge about cus­tomers in each lo­cale, and the best way to pro­duce there, ex­ists in­side the firm. In large, im­pe­rial firms it does not bub­ble up. {103-C15}

Often, he said, a top team is “thrilled to bits” at its own suc­cess and sure it has the one right an­swer for the whole world. It pushes or­ders down and stops lis­ten­ing, and pro­duc­tiv­ity suf­fers.

~ Varma added that big com­pa­nies often fail this way. Kodak had dig­i­tal pho­tog­ra­phy within the com­pany and did noth­ing with it. {#kodak} Incentives and silos played a part, he said, but so did truth fail­ing to travel up­ward.

quote.text: We’ve evolved to get along with each other. Right? We’ve not evolved to tell the truth.

When you build a suc­cess­ful busi­ness, the only way it can be suc­cess­ful is by pro­vid­ing value to peo­ple, by mak­ing in­di­vid­u­als bet­ter off, and even­tu­ally at scale mak­ing so­ci­ety bet­ter off.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A plane meal, one room, a lamp post and a lion

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on an airline crew that would not own up
stories.head: The vegan meal that wasn’t
body: Amit Varma likes watch­ing YouTube videos of lux­ury re­sorts and of busi­ness and first class on flights. A re­viewer he trusts is Nonstop Dan, who flies busi­ness class all year, pays for it him­self and makes videos of it.
The two times Varma has flown busi­ness class abroad, he chose the air­line from Dan’s videos, and got ex­actly the ex­pe­ri­ence Dan de­scribed, pros and cons in­cluded.
Two days be­fore the record­ing, Dan posted a video on Air India. Its new busi­ness class, he said, was ab­so­lutely awe­some: higher walls, more pri­vacy, a door you can close.

Then came the food. Dan had or­dered a spe­cial meal, a vegan one, Varma thinks, and it had not been loaded. The crew served him a dish and in­sisted it was his vegan meal. He read the in­gre­di­ents, found cheese, and pointed out that it was the reg­u­lar dish on the menu.
He kept ar­gu­ing. A su­pe­rior was called, and seemed just as lost. At the sec­ond meal, the same thing hap­pened.

Dan was fu­ri­ous, and Varma thought rightly so. In Varma’s telling, Dan asked: “What if I had a food al­lergy? What if I said I’m al­ler­gic to peanuts and there were peanuts in some­thing? And not only did these peo­ple not know it, they lied to me about it.” {103-S06}

~ The right an­swer, Varma said, was sim­ple: apol­o­gise, admit the meal had been for­got­ten, offer what was on board in econ­omy and first class, and make it up to him after the flight with a re­fund or points.
stories.why: A cul­ture of truth-telling has to be built, Varma ar­gued, be­cause hu­mans evolved to get along. The re­flex to cover up is the one that makes peo­ple on the street con­fi­dently give di­rec­tions they don’t know. {103-J19}
stories.postscript: Varma al­lows one ex­cep­tion. If your lady love asks whether she looks fat in a dress, “there is only one an­swer”. {103-J20}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Nonstop Dan’s missing meal

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a firm run by three founders in one room
stories.head: Three’s company at BillDesk
body: Garry Tan, Amit Varma said, warns against co-CEOs, be­cause two peo­ple must sign off on every de­ci­sion. Ajay Shah had a story that cuts the other way.

His friend Ajay Kaushal co-founded BillDesk, a very suc­cess­ful Indian firm. Its big exit was snarled up by Indian gov­ern­ment de­lays; but for that, Shah said, it would have been one of the big­gest exits in Indian his­tory.

Its three co-founders sit in one room and argue over every im­por­tant de­ci­sion, and none wants to be sole CEO. “So they think none of us is good enough to do it alone,” Shah said. They worked that way with no em­ploy­ees and still do with ten thou­sand. {103-S05}
~ Shah cred­its Kaushal’s char­ac­ter: quiet, unas­sum­ing and hum­ble, in­ter­ested in the idea and the ar­gu­ment, never in flaunt­ing his own glory. “Ajays are awe­some,” Varma said. {103-J12}
stories.why: Varma called it an out­lier, but a les­son all the same: a sin­gle CEO is not a hard and fast rule. Think for your­self, he said, from your val­ues and your own cir­cum­stances, rather than get­ting into a groove.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on BillDesk’s three founders

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells Simon Sinek’s story of Phil Knight
stories.head: Just do it, in the dark
body: At a con­fer­ence, Simon Sinek re­calls, Phil Knight of Nike asked ev­ery­one who ran for ex­er­cise to stand. Most of the room stood up. {103-R11}

Then he thinned them out, first those who ran less than once a week, then less than twice. Only those who ran at least three times a week, rain or shine, feel­ing good or bad, stayed stand­ing: a hand­ful.

The next time you are out be­fore dawn, Knight told them, “run­ning in the dark­ness and it’s wet and you’re feel­ing mis­er­able and you’re still run­ning”, and there is a guy under the lamp post cheer­ing you on, “that’s us”. {103-S03}
~ Amit Varma said the story moves him. With a brand like that, the story is no longer about sell­ing cool sneak­ers but about your per­son­al­ity, your dreams and who you are.

quote.text: Just do it is not about win­ning. It is about doing.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the guy under the lamp post

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why he works in bursts
stories.head: Sleep, sprint, repeat
body: Amit Varma has long lamented that, in Eisenhower’s ma­trix, he lives in two quad­rants: not im­por­tant and not ur­gent, or im­por­tant and ur­gent, as when an episode must be shot. Tim Urban, he said, wrote about the same dilemma. {103-R32}
Then came Naval Ravikant’s ad­vice: work like a lion. A lion sleeps eigh­teen hours and chills most of the time, then puts in a fu­ri­ous sprint. {#lion}

Humans were shaped in the hunter-gatherer age, Varma rea­soned, and fo­cus­ing hard burns calo­ries. “So it is nat­u­ral for us, it is ef­fi­cient for us, it is ra­tio­nal for us to get dis­tracted be­cause we save the calo­ries for the hunt.” {103-S10}
~ There is no right or wrong about it, he said. His fix: ac­cept the wiring, and use hacks such as cal­en­daris­ing to make the im­por­tant ur­gent.
stories.why: Seeing a flaw as evolved wiring re­moves the shame and points to work­arounds. The hosts teach the same in their course *Life Lessons*: am­plify what is good in our wiring and mit­i­gate what is bad.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on working like a lion

quiz.q: What did Bill Gates tell Mike Moritz had happened to the radio in his car?
quiz.a: He took it out him­self, so he could think about Microsoft.

quiz.q: Which word did Larry Page search for to show Excite what PageRank could do?
quiz.a: “University”: his en­gine found Harvard and Stanford, while Excite re­turned ran­dom junk.

quiz.q: How long did it take to integrate PayPal into a website, and how long Stripe?
quiz.a: About seven days, with a hun­dred-page man­ual; Stripe took five min­utes.

quiz.q: At Phil Knight’s talk, who is the guy under the lamp post cheering runners on?
quiz.a: Nike: the brand that is with you when you do, not only when you win.

quiz.q: What did Warren Buffett’s father teach him to be guided by?
quiz.a: His inner score­card of val­ues, not the outer one of money and rep­u­ta­tion.

quiz.q: According to Sam Altman, what is the only arbitrage opportunity left in the market?
quiz.a: A long-term com­mit­ment, when ev­ery­one else is chas­ing the next quar­ter.

glossary.def: Revising your be­liefs as new ev­i­dence, or a partner’s view, ar­rives.
Bezos’s rule: argue your case, then fully back the de­ci­sion.
Profiting from a gap in the mar­ket that oth­ers over­look.
A founder who starts and runs a busi­ness alone.
A paan seller, the land­mark in a con­fi­dent stranger’s di­rec­tions.
Varma’s gloss: in every com­mu­nity, most peo­ple are no good.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 103. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Sam Altman (Steve Jurvetson, CC BY 2.0); Mike Tyson (Super Festivals, CC BY 2.0); Eric Schmidt (Guillaume Paumier, CC BY 3.0); Brian Chesky (Celeste Sloman, CC BY-SA 4.0); Clayton Christensen (World Economic Forum from Cologny, Switzerland, CC BY-SA 2.0); Paul Graham (Sarah Harlin, public domain); Warren Buffett (Mark Hirschey, CC BY-SA 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: You Should Start a Business (Part 1)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It sets up this episode.

shelf.title: Sam Altman on being a generalist
shelf.creator: Sam Altman
shelf.why: Altman ar­gues you can be a spe­cial­ist while it’s a project, but the mo­ment you be­come a com­pany founder you must step back and think broadly.

shelf.title: Elon Musk on First-Principles Thinking
shelf.creator: Elon Musk
shelf.why: It is a con­crete ex­am­ple of pric­ing ma­te­ri­als from scratch, which took bat­tery costs from $600 to $80 per kWh against ex­pert con­sen­sus.

shelf.title: Aravind Srinivas speaks of Larry Page
shelf.creator: Aravind Srinivas
shelf.why: It tells the Larry Page and Excite story, and how it stopped Srinivas from blam­ing his own mother’s search phras­ing.

shelf.title: Garry Tan on acting small
shelf.creator: Garry Tan
shelf.why: Small com­pa­nies shouldn’t im­i­tate big-company pol­ish.

shelf.title: Kevin Hale on marketing
shelf.creator: Kevin Hale
shelf.why: ‘Marketing is a tax you pay for not mak­ing your prod­uct awesome’ cap­tures Amit’s prod­uct-first phi­los­o­phy.

shelf.title: Jeff Bezos product & marketing
shelf.creator: Jeff Bezos
shelf.why: Bezos de­scribes how, over his life­time, the focus has shifted from mar­ket­ing to prod­uct.

shelf.title: Naval Ravikant on networking
shelf.creator: Naval Ravikant
shelf.why: Networking is per­sonal mar­ket­ing.

shelf.title: Bezos on Akio Morita
shelf.creator: Jeff Bezos
shelf.why: Morita’s mis­sion, ‘make Japan known for qual­ity again’, is a model of a pur­pose big­ger than the prod­uct.

shelf.title: Patrick Collison on Stripe’s mission
shelf.creator: Patrick Collison
shelf.why: ‘Increase the GDP of the internet’ is an­other mis­sion big­ger than the com­pany it­self.

shelf.title: Simon Sinek on Nike’s mission
shelf.creator: Simon Sinek
shelf.why: It shows a brand built on ‘we are with you when you do’, not on sell­ing shoes.

shelf.title: Jensen Huang’s fish-pond metaphor
shelf.creator: Jensen Huang
shelf.why: Huang wasn’t try­ing to be a big fish in a small pond but to en­large the pond, cre­at­ing new mar­kets in­stead of fight­ing over old ones.

shelf.title: Altman on long-term thinking
shelf.creator: Sam Altman
shelf.why: ‘A long term com­mit­ment is the only ar­bi­trage op­por­tu­nity left in the market’ when ev­ery­one else chases the next quar­ter.

shelf.title: Bezos on business plans
shelf.creator: Jeff Bezos
shelf.why: Plans fall apart on con­tact with re­al­ity, but writ­ing them clar­i­fies your think­ing and pushes you to look ahead.

shelf.title: Vinod Khosla on vision & tactics
shelf.creator: Vinod Khosla
shelf.why: ‘Be ob­sti­nate about your vi­sion, but flex­i­ble about your tactics’ shows how long-term vi­sion and daily adap­ta­tion co­ex­ist.

shelf.title: Eric Schmidt on five-year plans
shelf.creator: Eric Schmidt
shelf.why: An econ­omy can’t be cen­trally planned but a com­pany can.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episodes on firms (incl. Family Firms; Imperial vs Decentralised Firms)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: Collison on choosing cofounders
shelf.creator: Patrick Collison
shelf.why: Starting a com­pany with some­one you’re close to is a fea­ture, not a bug.

shelf.title: Brian Chesky on co-founders
shelf.creator: Brian Chesky
shelf.why: You’ll spend more time with your co-founder than your spouse, and ‘win­ning an ar­gu­ment is not as im­por­tant as pre­serv­ing the relationship’.

shelf.title: Naval Ravikant on co-founder qualities
shelf.creator: Naval Ravikant
shelf.why: Look for high in­tel­li­gence, high en­ergy and high in­tegrity, and in­tegrity mat­ters most by far.

shelf.title: Tan on co-CEOs
shelf.creator: Garry Tan
shelf.why: Co-CEOs may suit the founders but slow every de­ci­sion for ev­ery­one below them.

shelf.title: Paul Graham on hiring
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Ten ran­dom row­ers make an av­er­age boat; the ten best make a much faster one.

shelf.title: Steve Jobs on hiring
shelf.creator: Steve Jobs
shelf.why: Everything de­pends on your first five hires.

shelf.title: Altman on hiring
shelf.creator: Sam Altman
shelf.why: Hire for val­ues first, ap­ti­tude sec­ond, skill third.

shelf.title: Mike Moritz on Bill Gates’s car radio
shelf.creator: Mike Moritz
shelf.why: Gates re­moved his car radio so he could think about Microsoft.

shelf.title: Huang on not wearing a watch
shelf.creator: Jensen Huang
shelf.why: ‘Now is the most im­por­tant time.’ Give what­ever you’re doing your full at­ten­tion.

shelf.title: Altman on burnout
shelf.creator: Sam Altman
shelf.why: Hard work doesn’t burn you out, be­cause mo­men­tum is en­er­gis­ing.

shelf.title: Bezos on Work-Life Harmony
shelf.creator: Jeff Bezos
shelf.why: Bezos re­jects ‘work-life balance’ for ‘work-life harmony’: go where the en­ergy is.

shelf.title: Huang on work & suffering
shelf.creator: Jensen Huang
shelf.why: Greatness in­volves suf­fer­ing.

shelf.title: Ravikant on working like a lion
shelf.creator: Naval Ravikant
shelf.why: Lions rest most of the time and then sprint.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: The Procrastination Matrix
shelf.creator: Tim Urban
shelf.why: Urban writes about ex­actly Amit’s dilemma: liv­ing in the ur­gent or the triv­ial quad­rants and never reach­ing the im­por­tant-but-not-urgent one.

shelf.title: Bezos on truth-telling
shelf.creator: Jeff Bezos
shelf.why: Humans evolved to get along, not to tell the truth, so com­pa­nies must de­lib­er­ately build mech­a­nisms and a cul­ture of truth-telling.

shelf.title: Bezos interviewed by Lex Fridman
shelf.creator: Lex Fridman
shelf.why: Here Bezos ex­plains ‘dis­agree and commit’: argue, then fully own the de­ci­sion with­out any ‘I told you so’ later.

shelf.title: Nonstop Dan on Air India
shelf.creator: Nonstop Dan
shelf.why: It is a live ex­am­ple of a crew lying about a miss­ing spe­cial meal in­stead of own­ing the mis­take.

shelf.title: Vlad Tenev’s product philosophy
shelf.creator: Vlad Tenev
shelf.why: ‘One screen, one but­ton, one action’ guards against throw­ing every good idea into the prod­uct.

shelf.title: Collison on beauty
shelf.creator: Patrick Collison
shelf.why: People like beau­ti­ful things.

shelf.title: Bezos on professional pride
shelf.creator: Jeff Bezos
shelf.why: 99% of your work will never be seen, so take pride in it any­way.

shelf.title: Warren Buffett on inner scorecards
shelf.creator: Warren Buffett
shelf.why: Buffett’s fa­ther taught him to live by his inner score­card of val­ues rather than the outer score­card of money and rep­u­ta­tion.

shelf.title: How Will You Measure Your Life?
shelf.creator: Clayton Christensen et al.
shelf.why: It ex­tends the idea of judg­ing your life by your own val­ues rather than ex­ter­nal suc­cess.

shelf.title: Startup Archive
shelf.creator: Startup Archive
shelf.why: An Instagram ac­count of founder and in­vestor ad­vice clips, the source of most of the ma­te­rial for the hosts’ episodes on start­ing a busi­ness; Amit counts many of these founders among today’s finest thinkers.

shelf.title: Paul Graham’s essays
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Free es­says that Amit calls ‘a trea­sure given to mankind’: mod­els of sim­ple, clear writ­ing, each work­shopped for months, by some­one who also builds things.

shelf.title: Sarkari Khatiya Private Karo
shelf.why: It is the comic set-piece that opens the episode.

laughs.text: The botched call-and-response. Amit: ‘Which game do you play, Ajay Shah?’ Ajay: ‘The hun­dred year game.’ Amit: ‘Why can’t you just re­peat what I said? There’s a nice po­etry to it.’ Take two: ‘The long game.’ ‘That’s how I like it. You’re fol­low­ing in­struc­tions.’
Professional pride, ap­plied: Amit boasts that the bacon and sour­dough he made for the crew the night be­fore ‘was the best bacon and sour­dough ever made in these climes in which we record.’

The mar­ket­ing-hater’s sign-off: ‘send them to all your friends, like, sub­scribe, and what­ever else you’re sup­posed to say. Did I just say I will never do mar­ket­ing? I will never do mar­ket­ing, don’t bother.’

Kipling’s ‘What do they know of England who only England know?’ and C.L.R. James’s cricket ver­sion, gen­er­alised by Amit to ‘What do they know of X who only X know?’ as the case for gen­er­al­ist founders.
Mike Tyson’s ‘Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face’, which Ajay sup­plies when Amit fum­bles it, used to frame Bezos’s ad­mit­tedly BS busi­ness plan.
